At last the narrow streets and courtyards opened onto a large space scattered with animal pens and other signs of a cattle market. Sikes slowed down there, for the girl could no longer keep up the fast pace at which they had been walking. He turned to Oliver and harshly ordered him to take Nancy’s hand.

“Did you hear me?” Sikes growled when Oliver hesitated and glanced around.

They stood in a dark corner, well away from anyone passing by.

Oliver could see all too clearly that resistance was useless. He held out his hand, and Nancy gripped it tightly.

“Give me the other,” Sikes said, grabbing Oliver’s free hand. “Here, Bull’s-eye!”

The dog looked up and growled.

“Look here, boy!” Sikes said, placing his other hand against Oliver’s throat. “If he says even one little word, grab him! Understand?”

The dog growled again, licked his lips, and watched Oliver as though eager to sink his teeth into the boy’s throat at once.

“He’s as willing as any Christian, strike me blind if he isn’t!” Sikes said, looking at the animal with fierce, grim approval. “Now you know what to expect, young master. Shout whenever you like; the dog will soon put a stop to that. Get moving, young fellow!”

Bull’s-eye wagged his tail at this unusually affectionate way of speaking. After another warning growl directed at Oliver, he led them onward.

They were crossing Smithfield, though for all Oliver knew they might have been in Grosvenor Square. The night was dark and foggy. Light from the shops could barely pierce the thick mist, which grew heavier every moment and wrapped the streets and houses in darkness. It made the unfamiliar place seem even stranger to Oliver and made his uncertainty still more frightening and miserable.

They had hurried a few steps farther when a deep church bell began striking the hour. At its first stroke, both his captors stopped and turned toward the sound.

“Eight o’clock, Bill,” Nancy said when the bell finished.

“What’s the use of telling me? I can hear it, can’t I?” Sikes answered.

“I wonder if they can hear it,” Nancy said.

“Of course they can,” Sikes replied. “It was Bartholomew Fair when I was arrested, and there wasn’t a cheap trumpet in the whole fair whose squeaking I couldn’t hear. Once I was locked up for the night, all the noise outside made that damned old jail seem so silent I could almost have smashed my brains out against the iron plates on the door.”

“But,” I said, handing the slip back, “I am as much in the dark as before. Even if solving this puzzle would earn me every jewel in Golconda, I am certain I could never claim the reward.”

“And yet,” Legrand said, “the solution is nowhere near as difficult as a quick first glance at the symbols might suggest. As anyone could easily guess, these symbols form a cipher: they carry a meaning. But from what we know of Kidd, I could hardly imagine him devising one of the more intricate codes. I immediately decided it must be a simple kind, though one that a sailor’s untrained mind would consider completely impossible to solve without the key.”

“And you actually solved it?”

“Easily. I have solved others ten thousand times more complicated. Circumstances, together with a particular turn of mind, have drawn me to such puzzles, and I seriously doubt whether human ingenuity can create a cipher that human ingenuity, properly applied, cannot unravel. In fact, once I had established a connected sequence of readable symbols, I hardly thought about the difficulty of working out what they meant.

“In this case—as in every case of secret writing—the first question concerns the cipher’s language. The methods of solving it, especially with simpler ciphers, depend on the distinctive character of the language and vary accordingly. Usually, the only option is to try every language the investigator knows, guided by what seems most likely, until the right one is found. Here, though, the signature removed that difficulty altogether. The pun on ‘Kidd’ makes sense only in English. Without that clue I would have started with Spanish and French, since a pirate of the Spanish Main would most naturally have recorded this kind of secret in one of those languages. As it was, I assumed the coded message was English.

“You will notice that there are no spaces between the words. If there had been, the task would have been relatively easy. In that situation I would have started by comparing and analyzing the shorter words. If a word consisting of a single letter had appeared, as would be very likely—‘a’ or ‘I,’ for example—I would have considered the solution certain. But since there were no word divisions, my first step was to identify the letters that occurred most often, along with those that appeared least frequently.”

Yet even then I had not drained the bitter cup to its last drop; I had not fully believed my loss; I did not yet know in every pulse, every nerve, every thought, that I alone survived of my race—that I was the LAST MAN.

Clouds had gathered over the day, and at sunset a fine rain began to fall. Even the everlasting heavens shed tears, I thought; why, then, should mortal man be ashamed to exhaust himself in weeping? I recalled the ancient tales in which human creatures melt through their tears into fountains that flow forever. Ah, if only it could be so! Then my fate would in some measure resemble the watery deaths of Adrian and Clara. Oh, grief has strange fancies; it spins a web on which every shape and change around it inscribes the story of its sorrow. It mingles with all living nature and draws nourishment from every object; like light, it enters everything, and like light, lends everything its own hues.

My search had carried me some distance from the place where I had been cast ashore, until I reached one of the watchtowers standing at regular intervals along the Italian coast. I welcomed shelter, and welcomed a structure made by human hands after gazing so long upon nature’s desolate emptiness. Entering, I climbed the rough spiral stairs to the guardroom. Fate was kind this far: no distressing remnant of its former occupants remained. A few boards resting on two iron trestles, scattered with dried maize leaves, offered me a bed. An open chest holding some half-moldy biscuits stirred an appetite that perhaps had existed earlier, though I had not recognized it until now. A fierce, scorching thirst also tormented me, caused by the seawater I had swallowed and my body’s exhaustion. Kindly nature had attached pleasure to the satisfaction of these needs, so that I—even I!—grew refreshed and calmer while eating that wretched food and drinking a little sour wine from a half-filled flask left in the deserted dwelling. Then I lay down upon the bed, which no shipwrecked sufferer could scorn. After the loathsome smell of seaweed, the earthy scent of the dry leaves soothed my senses. I forgot my solitude. I looked neither behind me nor ahead; my senses settled into quiet rest. I slept and dreamed of beloved inland scenes: haymakers, a shepherd whistling to summon his dog’s help in driving the flock into the fold, and the sights and sounds of my childhood among the mountains, which I had long since forgotten.
